title: How many of your students are participating?
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton argues that low student participation, not the usual suspects of challenge, curriculum or assessment, is the hidden constraint holding back most of the lessons he observes. Building on Doug Lemov's participation ratio, he sharpens the idea into three questions: how many students are listening, thinking and understanding, and how does the teacher know. He then breaks a lesson into five phases (retrieval Do Now, prerequisite check, explanation and worked example, practice, plenary) and sets teachers a self-audit exercise rating each phase high, medium or low. The move of the piece is to re-test those ratings against his observations, showing how common routines such as calling on one student and having the rest correct in green pen leave most of the class invisible. He singles out the explanation phase as typically the weakest and uses a congruency plenary to show how little a teacher can infer from two volunteered answers. Classified Learning & Curriculum because the argument is about checking for understanding and formative assessment within lesson design.
points: Barton reports that schools never name participation as a development priority, yet in almost every school he visits it is the thing that must be fixed before other improvements can land.
The participation ratio is made concrete through three evidence questions, listening, thinking and understanding, each followed by 'how do you know?'
Routine Do Now review, where one student answers and the rest self-correct, is shown to reveal nothing about the other 29 students and invites 'Busy Tricking'.
Barton identifies the explanation and worked-example phase as usually having the lowest participation, since a few students answer while the majority smile and nod.
Going through answers during practice can mask misunderstanding: a student who had corrected an answer in green pen could not explain why, and neither student nor teacher knew.
quotes: It is often around stretch and challenge, curriculum design, assessment, or modelling. It is never - and I repeat, never - around student participation. And yet, in almost every school I visit, it is the student participation in lessons - or, more precisely, the lack of it - that is holding back teaching and learning.

Unless students are listening to our instructions, explanations or the answers of their classmates, everything we do is a waste of time. Now, it is obvious that the student talking to his neighbour during your explanation is not listening.

Sure, they might be thinking hard about our instructions, explanation, the question we have asked, the task we have set, or the response of their classmate, but how do we know for sure? How do we know that they are not daydreaming, safe in the knowledge that we are unlikely to ask them as they are one student in a class of thirty?

Sure, they know something about the thinking and understanding of the one child who answered the question, but how about the other 29? Could they have got away with doing little to no thinking during the Do Now, safe in the knowledge they can now just copy down the correct answer? Might they now be confused and yet are reluctant to say?

In my experience, the explanation or modelling phase of the lesson is the one with the lowest participation ratio. Often it is teacher-dominated, with students' role being to sit there quietly and then copy whatever is on the board into their book when told - see my previous post on the Myth of Copying Things Down for more on this.
I asked the student to explain to me why their answer was wrong and how to get the correct answer. They didn't have a clue. How many students in the class were in a similar position?

The teacher rounded-up the explanation given, congratulated the student, and then the class left the room. How many students were thinking hard about the answer? How many were listening to the student's explanation?
